content: Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for malaria have limitations, including poor sensitivity in detecting Plasmodium malariae and Plasmodium ovale, as well as inconsistent quality among commercially available products, with variations between production batches. A systematic review compared the sensitivity and specificity of RDTs for detecting Plasmodium falciparum in blood samples from symptomatic patients in malaria-endemic areas with microscopy and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). While RDTs are effective, their performance can vary depending on the type of test and the parasite density. Studies have shown that healthcare workers, volunteers, and private sector providers can use RDTs accurately with proper training and supervision. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides criteria for selecting and procuring RDTs on its website. Accurate malaria diagnosis using microscopy or RDTs is essential to reduce the overuse of antimalarial medicines by ensuring treatment is only given to patients with confirmed malaria infections, rather than treating all febrile patients presumptively. However, healthcare providers do not always respond appropriately to negative test results, which can lead to mismanagement of febrile illnesses. Advanced molecular techniques, such as PCR and loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP), are highly sensitive and useful for detecting mixed infections, particularly at low parasite densities that are undetectable by conventional microscopy or RDTs. These methods are also valuable for studying drug resistance and conducting specialized epidemiological investigations. However, they are not widely available for large-scale field use in endemic areas and are not suitable for routine diagnosis in regions with high prevalence of low-density parasitemia. These techniques may be useful for population surveys and malaria elimination programs but currently have no role in routine clinical management or surveillance systems. Prompt and accurate malaria diagnosis is critical for effective disease management. All patients with suspected malaria should be treated based on a confirmed diagnosis using microscopy or RDTs. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups, such as young children and non-immune populations, where Plasmodium falciparum malaria can be rapidly fatal. High specificity in diagnosis reduces unnecessary antimalarial treatment and improves the identification of other febrile illnesses. WHO strongly advocates a test, treat, and track policy to enhance care quality and surveillance. The primary therapeutic goal in treating uncomplicated malaria is to cure the infection quickly and prevent progression to severe disease. Cure is defined as the complete elimination of parasites from the body. Public health objectives include preventing onward transmission of the infection and minimizing the emergence and spread of drug resistance. The use of monotherapy, such as artemisinin derivatives or partner medicines alone, is discouraged as it promotes drug resistance. Incomplete dosing of antimalarial drugs is another concern. In endemic regions, some semi-immune patients may recover with incomplete treatment, but this practice is no longer recommended. A full course of highly effective ACT is required for all patients, regardless of their immune status. Administering only the first dose of treatment to patients with suspected but unconfirmed malaria is unsafe, can promote resistance, and is not recommended. For patients unable to tolerate oral medication, parenteral or rectal administration is required for 1–2 days until oral treatment can be reliably administered. These patients should receive the same initial antimalarial treatments recommended for severe malaria, followed by a full 3-day course of ACT. Antipyretics are used to manage high fevers, particularly in young children, to prevent complications such as vomiting, regurgitation of medication, and seizures. Paracetamol is preferred due to its safety profile, while ibuprofen and aspirin are no longer recommended due to risks of gastrointestinal bleeding, renal impairment, and Reye’s syndrome. Vomiting is common in acute malaria and may necessitate parenteral antimalarial treatment until oral administration is tolerated. Anti-emetics should be used cautiously as they may have sedative effects and could mask or confound the diagnosis of severe malaria. Seizures, more common in children with Plasmodium falciparum malaria, may indicate cerebral malaria. Patients experiencing multiple seizures within 24 hours should be treated as having severe malaria. Anticonvulsants, such as benzodiazepines or paraldehyde, may be administered if seizures persist. ACTs combine a fast-acting artemisinin derivative with a longer-acting partner drug. The artemisinin component rapidly clears parasites from the blood and is also active against gametocytes, reducing onward transmission to mosquitoes. The partner drug eliminates remaining parasites and provides protection against resistance development. WHO recommends several ACT options for treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, and artesunate-sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. These options are suitable for adults, children, infants, lactating women, and pregnant women in their second and third trimesters. National policymakers should consider drug resistance patterns, efficacy, safety, cost, and availability when selecting ACTs for firstand second-line treatments. Dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine is recommended for general use due to its high efficacy and long half-life, which provides post-treatment prophylaxis. However, concerns about QT interval prolongation have been noted, and further studies are needed to assess its safety, particularly in young children. Artesunate-pyronaridine is another ACT option, but it should be avoided in individuals with known liver disease due to its association with liver enzyme elevations. Pharmacovigilance and resistance surveillance systems should be strengthened wherever new treatments are introduced. Shorter courses are less effective and provide insufficient protection for the partner drug. In summary, WHO guidelines advocate for the use of ACTs as the cornerstone of malaria treatment, with a focus on accurate diagnosis, complete treatment courses, and careful monitoring of drug safety and efficacy. Strengthening pharmacovigilance and resistance surveillance is critical to maintaining the effectiveness of these therapies.
